entries.title: A face praised, a body judged
entries.literal_meaning: The face is beautiful; the body is ugly.
entries.explanation: The parallel halves divide one person into a praised face and a disparaged body. The dictionary places the last word under “ugly,” not its other senses of a lump or something flat. Our critical reading asks what this splitting does to the person being described. The source supplies the appearance judgment; our objection to reducing someone to it is editorial.
entries.meaning_odia: ସମାନ ଢାଞ୍ଚାର ଦୁଇ ଖଣ୍ଡ ଜଣେ ମଣିଷକୁ ପ୍ରଶଂସିତ ମୁହଁ ଓ ନିନ୍ଦିତ ଦେହରେ ବାଣ୍ଟେ। ଅଭିଧାନ ଶେଷ ଶବ୍ଦକୁ ଅସୁନ୍ଦର ଅର୍ଥରେ ରଖିଛି, ମେଞ୍ଚା ବା ଚେପ୍ଟା ଅର୍ଥରେ ନୁହେଁ। ଆମ ସମାଲୋଚନାତ୍ମକ ପଢ଼ା ପଚାରେ—ଏହି ବାଣ୍ଟିବା ବର୍ଣ୍ଣିତ ଲୋକଟିକୁ କେଉଁଠି ରଖେ? ରୂପର ରାୟ ଉତ୍ସରେ ଅଛି; ମଣିଷକୁ ସେତିକିରେ ସୀମିତ କରିବା ପ୍ରତି ଆପତ୍ତି ଆମର।
entries.english_summary: Our critical reading questions dividing a person into praised and disparaged features.
entries.odia_summary: ପ୍ରଶଂସା ଓ ନିନ୍ଦାର ଅଙ୍ଗରେ ମଣିଷକୁ ବାଣ୍ଟିବା ପ୍ରତି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A reading group discusses appearance-based remarks. One participant quotes the line; another asks how the person described might feel hearing praise immediately turned into an insult. This imagined discussion questions the judgment rather than describing an actual person.
entries.cultural_context: A short dictionary-labelled expression, not a diagnosis or objective measure of beauty. No gender, body type or community is assigned beyond what the wording establishes.

entries.title: Noble words and the person behind them
entries.literal_meaning: A noble person’s noble words—or deeds.
entries.explanation: The repeated word links the person with what they say or do. The dictionary gives both words and acts among the headword’s senses. Our reading can hear straightforward appreciation of generosity; the source does not fix an ironic tone or make wealth and rank the measure of nobility. The brief expression leaves the particular act unnamed.
entries.meaning_odia: ମହତ ଶବ୍ଦର ପୁନରାବୃତ୍ତି ଲୋକଟି ସହ ତାଙ୍କ କଥା ବା କାମକୁ ଯୋଡ଼େ। ଅଭିଧାନ ଶବ୍ଦଟିର ଅର୍ଥରେ ଉଦାର ବାକ୍ୟ ଓ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟ ଉଭୟ ଦିଏ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଉଦାରତାର ସରଳ ପ୍ରଶଂସା ଶୁଣାଯାଇପାରେ; ଉତ୍ସ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗର ସ୍ୱର ସ୍ଥିର କରେନାହିଁ, ଧନ ବା ପଦକୁ ମହତ୍ତ୍ୱର ମାପ ମଧ୍ୟ କରେନାହିଁ। ଛୋଟ କଥାଟି ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦିଷ୍ଟ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟର ନାମ ଛାଡ଼ି ଦିଏ।
entries.english_summary: The repetition can praise generous words or conduct without specifying status.
entries.odia_summary: ପୁନରାବୃତ୍ତିରେ ଉଦାର କଥା ବା କାମର ପ୍ରଶଂସା ହୋଇପାରେ।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: At a club discussion, a member offers to share credit for a successful project with the quieter volunteers. Another recalls the noble-person expression in appreciation. The occasion and appreciative delivery are invented, not a documented traditional setting.
entries.cultural_context: Short dictionary-labelled expression with multiple lexical senses, not a recovered longer proverb. Neither mandatory irony nor a hereditary rank or community trait is established.

entries.title: An invitation to make trouble
entries.literal_meaning: If you have no quarrel, take two wives; if the rice does not run out, keep two residences.
entries.explanation: The paired invitations offer ways to acquire trouble or use up provisions. Our reading hears irony rather than practical instruction. It also questions the first half’s gendered assumption: conflict is assigned to a marriage arrangement without hearing the people involved. The second half turns to the cost of maintaining two places. Neither household outcome is demonstrated by the saying.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦୁଇଟି ନିମନ୍ତ୍ରଣ ଝଗଡ଼ା ଆଣିବା ବା ଖାଦ୍ୟ ସରାଇବାର ଉପାୟ ରଖେ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଏହା ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ, ବ୍ୟବହାରିକ ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦେଶ ନୁହେଁ। ପ୍ରଥମ ଖଣ୍ଡର ଲିଙ୍ଗଭିତ୍ତିକ ଧାରଣାକୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆମେ ପଚାରୁଛୁ—ସମ୍ପୃକ୍ତ ଲୋକଙ୍କ କଥା ନ ଶୁଣି ବିବାହର ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥାରେ ଝଗଡ଼ା ଧରାଯାଉଛି। ଦ୍ୱିତୀୟ ଖଣ୍ଡ ଦୁଇ ସ୍ଥାନ ଚଳାଇବାର ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚକୁ ଆଣେ। କୌଣସି ପରିବାରର ଫଳାଫଳ ଏହା ପ୍ରମାଣ କରେନାହିଁ।
entries.english_summary: Our reading hears ironic invitations to trouble while questioning the gendered premise.
entries.odia_summary: ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗାତ୍ମକ ନିମନ୍ତ୍ରଣ ସହ ଲିଙ୍ଗଭିତ୍ତିକ ଧାରଣା ପ୍ରତି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a discussion of exaggerated advice, a reader quotes the paired invitations. Another notes the extra work of maintaining two places, then asks why the marriage half treats quarrelling as inevitable. This is an invented critical conversation, not household or legal advice.
entries.cultural_context: The source defines two residences. Its marriage language is historical evidence, not a recommendation, claim about women’s nature or account of present law or universal custom.
